node.TEXT: Unit 3: Synchronization in Distributed Computing
1. Introduction
Challenges in Distributed Systems
Synchronization is much more difficult compared to uniprocessor/multiprocessor systems.
Two clocks do not agree perfectly.
Time synchronization is required for Correctness and Fairness.
Needed for sender-receiver sync and coordination of joint activity.
[DIAGRAM TO STUDY: Clock Synchronization issue - output.c vs output.o compile mismatch due to clock differences]
Clock Skew vs. Clock Drift
Clock Skew: Relative difference in clock values of two processes (like distance between two vehicles).
Clock Drift: Relative difference in clock frequencies of two processes (like difference in speeds).
A non-zero clock skew implies clocks are not synchronized.
A non-zero clock drift causes skew to increase.
For a perfect clock, skew = drift = 0.
Handling Skew
If clock is behind: run it faster.
If clock is ahead: run it slower.
Must check and adjust periodically.
Inaccuracies arise from delays in message transmission, processing time, and server inaccuracy.
External vs. Internal Synchronization
External Synchronization: Each process clock is within a bound D of a well-known external clock S (e.g., UTC). Examples: Cristian's Algorithm, NTP.
Internal Synchronization: Every pair of processes in a group have clocks within bound D of each other. Example: Berkeley Algorithm.
2. Physical Clocks
Basic Concepts
Computer timer uses a machined quartz crystal oscillating at a well-defined frequency.
Components: 2 registers (a counter and a holding register). Oscillation decrements counter. At zero, interrupt generated (one clock tick), and counter reloads.
Drift Rate (rho): The rate at which a computer clock deviates from a perfect reference clock.
Specification constraint: 1 - rho <= dC/dt <= 1 + rho.
To guarantee no two clocks differ by more than delta, resynchronize every delta / (2 * rho) seconds.
[DIAGRAM TO STUDY: Relation between clock time and UTC when clocks tick at different rates]
Time Standards
Astronomical Time: Solar day / Solar second.
International Atomic Time (TAI): Based on cesium 133 atom transitions. Introduces leap seconds to align with solar time.
Universal Coordinated Time (UTC): Basis of modern civil timekeeping. Broadcasted via shortwave radio and GPS.
Cristian's Algorithm (1989)
Attempt to compensate for network delays.
Client requests time, server replies with Ts.
Client notes local time before sending (T0) and after receiving (T1).
Correct time estimate: Ts + (T1 - T0) / 2 (Assumes symmetric network delay).
[DIAGRAM TO STUDY: Cristian's Algorithm client-server exchange and example calculation]
The Berkeley Algorithm
Time server (time daemon) is ACTIVE, unlike NTP/Cristian's where it is passive.
Daemon polls every machine to ask their time, calculates average, and tells everyone how to adjust.
Suitable when no machine has an accurate/reference clock.
Daemon's time must be manually set periodically by operator.
[DIAGRAM TO STUDY: 3-part Berkeley algorithm diagram (daemon asks, machines answer, daemon tells adjustment)]
Network Time Protocol (NTP)
Based on Cristian's algorithm but protocol is setup pair-wise between servers.
Finds good estimate for message delays without making the clock go backward.
Message flow: A requests at T1, B receives at T2, B responds at T3, A receives at T4.
Offset (theta): (T2 - T1) + (T3 - T4) / 2.
Delay (delta): (T2 - T1) + (T4 - T3) / 2.
Buffers eight pairs of (theta, delta) and takes minimal values as best estimation.
Divides servers into STRATA. Stratum-1 has reference clock. A contacts B and adjusts only if A's stratum is higher (lower priority) than B's.
3. Logical Clocks
Focus is on internal consistency: agreeing on the ORDER in which events occur, not the actual real time.
Lamport's Logical Clocks
Defines happens-before relation (a -> b).
1. If events a and b are in the same process, and a occurs before b, then a -> b.
2. If a is a message sent and b is message received, a -> b.
3. Transitive: If a -> b and b -> c, then a -> c.
Properties: If a -> b, then C(a) < C(b). Clock C must always go forward.
1. Before executing an event, process Pi executes Ci = Ci + 1.
2. Pi sends message m with timestamp ts(m) = Ci.
3. Pj receives m, updates clock: Cj = max(Cj, ts(m)), then executes Cj = Cj + 1 and delivers.
[DIAGRAM TO STUDY: Lamport logical clocks examples (events a-g, correction of clocks running at different rates, and middleware layer positioning)]
Example: Totally Ordered Multicasting
Ensures all messages are delivered in the same order to each receiver (e.g., replicated database updates A=100, B=100).
Process multicasts timestamped message. Receiver puts it in local queue ordered by timestamp.
Receiver multicasts an acknowledgement.
Message delivered to application only when at head of queue AND fully acknowledged.
Vector Clocks
Lamport clocks drawback: C(a) < C(b) does not guarantee that a causally preceded b.
Vector clock property: If VC(a) < VC(b), then 'a' is known to causally precede 'b'.
Process Pi maintains vector VCi.
VCi[i] = local logical clock of Pi (number of events at Pi).
VCi[j] = Pi's knowledge of the local time at Pj.
Implementation Steps
1. Before event, Pi executes VCi[i] = VCi[i] + 1.
2. Pi sends message m with vector timestamp ts(m) = VCi.
3. Pj receives m, updates: VCj[k] = max(VCj[k], ts(m)[k]) for each k, then executes first step.
[DIAGRAM TO STUDY: Vector Clocks Example tracking p1, p2, p3 arrays (e.g., (1,0,0), (2,1,0), etc.)]
4. Mutual Exclusion
Ensures concurrent processes access shared resources in a serialized way (no overlapping critical sections).
Two Categories
Token-based solutions: Token holder accesses resource. Avoids starvation and deadlocks. Drawback: Token loss.
Permission-based approach: Requires permission from other processes first.
Types of Algorithms
Centralized Algorithm
One process is coordinator. Request -> OK -> Access -> Release.
Advantages: Guarantees mutual exclusion, fair (queue), no starvation, easy to implement, needs only 3 messages.
Shortcomings: Single point of failure, dead coordinator vs permission denied confusion, performance bottleneck.
[DIAGRAM TO STUDY: Centralized Mutual Exclusion]
Decentralized Algorithm
Voting based on DHT system. Resource replicated n times.
Needs majority vote from m > n/2 coordinators.
If denied, back off for random time and retry.
Drawback: Starvation/low efficiency if many nodes want access simultaneously (no one gets majority).
Distributed Algorithm (Ricart and Agrawala's)
Requires total ordering of events.
Process broadcasts request (resource name, process number, logical time).
Receiver action based on 3 cases:
1. Not accessing & doesn't want: Sends OK.
2. Already has access: No reply, queues the request.
3. Wants access but hasn't yet: Compares timestamps. Lowest timestamp wins (sender gets OK if lower, else receiver queues).
Advantages: Deadlock-free, Starvation-free, no single point of failure. Messages per entry: 2(n-1).
Disadvantages: n points of failure, complicated, slower, group membership maintenance required.
[DIAGRAM TO STUDY: Distributed Algorithm 3-node example]
Token Ring Algorithm
Logical ring constructed (ordering doesn't matter, just needs successor).
Token circulates. If acquired and needs access -> executes, then passes. If no access needed -> just passes.
Advantages: Simple, deadlock-free. Messages: 1 to infinity. Delay: 0 to n-1.
Disadvantages: Token loss needs regeneration, process crash breaks ring (recovery needed).
[DIAGRAM TO STUDY: Unordered network vs Logical ring constructed in software]

5. Election Algorithms
Needed when distributed algorithms require a coordinator process.
Assumes each process has a unique number. Locates process with highest number to be coordinator.
Assumes every process knows the process number of every other process.
The Bully Algorithm
Triggered when coordinator stops responding.
Process P sends ELECTION message to all processes with HIGHER numbers.
If no one responds, P wins and becomes coordinator.
If a higher-up answers, it takes over the election process, and P's job is done.
[DIAGRAM TO STUDY: Bully Algorithm steps (nodes 0-6 holding elections, node 6 wins and tells everyone)]
A Ring Algorithm
Processes are physically or logically ordered (knows successor). Does NOT use a token.
Notices crash -> Builds ELECTION message with own ID -> Sends to successor.
Each step: process adds its own ID to the message list.
When message returns to starter, message type changed to COORDINATOR.
Circulates again to inform everyone of the new coordinator (member in the list with highest ID), then message is removed.
[DIAGRAM TO STUDY: Election algorithm using a ring (nodes converting ELECTION to COORDINATOR messages)]
